Yes, many animals demonstrate some degree of understanding of human language, though the extent varies by species and individual. [d3] Scientific research has found that 30 bird species and 29 mammal species share the same patterns of pitch and speed in basic messages, allowing humans and those species to mutually understand expressions of "aggression, hostility, appeasement, approachability, submission and fear." [d4] A study has also shown that dogs and many other species have the ability to process and understand words, with Chaser the Border Collie knowing the names of 1,022 different items. [d1] Beyond dogs, scientists have proven that some apes and dolphins can understand spoken language; for example, Kanzi the bonobo demonstrated understanding of more than 3,000 English words, tested by a researcher speaking from a separate room to avoid contextual clues. [d2] Other species such as potbelly pigs, chimpanzees, and elephants also understand some human language, and Koko the gorilla famously learned 2,000 words in American Sign Language, even using them to tell jokes and express emotions. [d3] Grey parrot Alex further illustrates this capacity, having learned 100 words and used them to correctly answer questions about color, shape, size, and numbers about 80% of the time. Overall, while no animal understands human language with the full complexity that humans do, the evidence across species shows a genuine, scientifically documented capacity for language comprehension in many animals [d1][d4].
